intro.title: Saved queries: views
intro.bodyMarkdown:
This section's database is a garden centre: `staff` (each with a `manager_id`), `categories` (inside other categories), `products` (with extra `details` stored as JSON), `sales`, and `targets` for each quarter. Open **Tables** to see them.

A **view** is a query with a name. Once it is made, you can select from it as if it were a table:

```
CREATE VIEW sale_lines AS
SELECT s.id AS sale_id, s.sold_on, p.name AS product, s.quantity
FROM sales s
JOIN products p ON p.id = s.product_id;

SELECT * FROM sale_lines WHERE quantity >= 3 ORDER BY sale_id;
```

A view stores the query, not the rows. Each time you select from it, the query runs again, so it always shows the data as it is now. That makes views good for queries you use often, and for hiding a long join behind a simple name.

The view's columns are named by the query, so name calculated columns with `AS`, or list the names after the view's name: `CREATE VIEW top_sellers (product, sold) AS SELECT …`.

Views can be used anywhere a table can in a SELECT: in joins, in subqueries, and in other views. You can't INSERT into a view or UPDATE it in SQLite: change the tables underneath instead.

To change a view, drop it and make it again: SQLite has no `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW`. `DROP VIEW sale_lines;` removes it (the tables stay as they are), and `CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS` skips the CREATE when the view is already there.

       SUM(s.quantity) AS items,
       ROUND(SUM(s.quantity * p.price), 2) AS takings
FROM sales s
JOIN products p ON p.id = s.product_id
LEFT JOIN categories c ON c.id = p.category_id
GROUP BY COALESCE(c.name, 'No category');

intro.title: Recursive WITH: making rows
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A CTE marked `RECURSIVE` can select from itself. That lets a query make rows that are in no table, such as the numbers 1 to 5:

```
WITH RECURSIVE n(x) AS (
  SELECT 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT x + 1 FROM n WHERE x < 5
)
SELECT x FROM n;
```

It has two parts joined by `UNION ALL`. The first, the **anchor**, gives the starting rows: here one row, 1. The second, the **recursive part**, is run on the rows made last time, and its rows are added: 2, then 3, and so on. When it makes no new rows, the recursion stops. The names in brackets after `n` name its columns.

The `WHERE x < 5` is what stops it. Leave it out and the query never ends, so always write the stop condition first. (A `LIMIT` on the final SELECT also stops it, as long as that SELECT has no `ORDER BY`, which would wait for every row first.)

The rows can be anything you can work out from the row before: dates with `date(day, '+1 day')`, amounts that double, text that grows. The anchor and the stop condition can read real tables, so this makes every day from the first sale to the last:

```
WITH RECURSIVE days(day) AS (
  SELECT MIN(sold_on) FROM sales
  UNION ALL
  SELECT date(day, '+1 day') FROM days
  WHERE day < (SELECT MAX(sold_on) FROM sales)
)
SELECT day FROM days ORDER BY day;
```

The rows come out in the order they were made, but only an `ORDER BY` guarantees an order, so add one when the order matters.

challenges.title: Easy: Count to the products
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the numbers (`x`) from 1 up to the number of products, in order.
challenges.hint: Stop with `WHERE x < (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products)`.

challenges.title: Easy: Every sales day
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show every date (`day`) from the first sale to the last, sales or not, in order.
challenges.hint: Start at `MIN(sold_on)`, add `date(day, '+1 day')`, stop at `MAX(sold_on)`.
challenges.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE days(day) AS (
  SELECT MIN(sold_on) FROM sales
  UNION ALL
  SELECT date(day, '+1 day') FROM days
  WHERE day < (SELECT MAX(sold_on) FROM sales)
)
SELECT day FROM days ORDER BY day;

challenges.title: Easy: Every other day
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show every second date (`day`) starting at the first sale, up to the last sale, in order.
challenges.hint: `date(day, '+2 days')`, and keep going while the next date isn't past the last sale.
challenges.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE days(day) AS (
  SELECT MIN(sold_on) FROM sales
  UNION ALL
  SELECT date(day, '+2 days') FROM days
  WHERE date(day, '+2 days') <= (SELECT MAX(sold_on) FROM sales)
)
SELECT day FROM days ORDER BY day;

challenges.title: Medium: Price ladder
challenges.promptMarkdown: For the cheapest product, show what 1 to 5 of it cost: `quantity` and `cost` (2 decimals). In order of quantity.
challenges.hint: Make 1 to 5, then multiply by `(SELECT MIN(price) FROM products)`.
challenges.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE q(quantity) AS (
  SELECT 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT quantity + 1 FROM q WHERE quantity < 5
)
SELECT quantity, ROUND(quantity * (SELECT MIN(price) FROM products), 2) AS cost
FROM q
ORDER BY quantity;

challenges.title: Medium: The next five days
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the five dates (`day`) after the last sale, using `LIMIT` to stop the recursion instead of a WHERE.
challenges.hint: Start one day after `MAX(sold_on)`, with no WHERE in the recursive part, and end with `SELECT day FROM days LIMIT 5`. Don't add ORDER BY: it would need every row first, and there is no end.

challenges.title: Medium: Weeks
challenges.promptMarkdown: Split the sales period into weeks starting on the first sale's date: `week_start` and `week_end` (6 days later), for every week that starts on or before the last sale. In order.
challenges.hint: Step by `'+7 days'` and show `date(week_start, '+6 days') AS week_end`.
challenges.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE weeks(week_start) AS (
  SELECT MIN(sold_on) FROM sales
  UNION ALL
  SELECT date(week_start, '+7 days') FROM weeks
  WHERE date(week_start, '+7 days') <= (SELECT MAX(sold_on) FROM sales)
)
SELECT week_start, date(week_start, '+6 days') AS week_end
FROM weeks
ORDER BY week_start;

challenges.title: Hard: Doubling
challenges.promptMarkdown: Start at the cheapest product's price and keep doubling it. Show each `step` (0 for the start) and `amount`, for as long as the amount is 100 or less. In order of step.
challenges.hint: Two columns in the CTE: `(step, amount)`. The recursive part keeps rows where `amount * 2 <= 100`.

challenges.title: Hard: Letter by letter
challenges.promptMarkdown: Split the name of the person at the top (no manager) into its characters: `n` (1 for the first) and `letter`, spaces included. In order of n.
challenges.hint: Count n from 1 up to `length(name)`, and take `substr(name, n, 1)`.
challenges.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE n(n) AS (
  SELECT 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM n WHERE n < (SELECT length(name) FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NULL)
)
SELECT n, substr((SELECT name FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NULL), n, 1) AS letter
FROM n
ORDER BY n;

challenges.title: Expert: Fibonacci
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the Fibonacci numbers 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, … that are no bigger than the number of sales: `n` (1 for the first) and `fib`. In order of n.
challenges.hint: Carry two numbers: `(n, fib, next_fib)` starting at `(1, 1, 1)`, then `(n + 1, next_fib, fib + next_fib)` while `next_fib <=` the count.
challenges.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE f(n, fib, next_fib) AS (
  SELECT 1, 1, 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1, next_fib, fib + next_fib FROM f
  WHERE next_fib <= (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sales)
)
SELECT n, fib FROM f ORDER BY n;

intro.title: Walking trees
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Each staff member's `manager_id` points to another row of `staff`, and their manager has a manager too, up to the person at the top. Data like that is a **tree**. A join finds one step; a recursive CTE follows all of them.

```
WITH RECURSIVE chart(id, name, level) AS (
  SELECT id, name, 1 FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.id, s.name, c.level + 1
  FROM staff s
  JOIN chart c ON s.manager_id = c.id
)
SELECT name, level FROM chart ORDER BY level, name;
```

The anchor is the top of the tree, the person with no manager, at level 1. The recursive part joins `staff` to the rows found so far: everyone whose manager is in `chart` is one level further down. It stops when a level finds nobody new.

The same pattern builds paths. Carry text along and add to it at each step, and you get each category's full path:

```
WITH RECURSIVE tree(id, path) AS (
  SELECT id, name FROM categories WHERE parent_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, t.path || ' > ' || c.name
  FROM categories c
  JOIN tree t ON c.parent_id = t.id
)
SELECT path FROM tree ORDER BY path;
```

You can also start anywhere and walk up: anchor on one person, and join to the manager of the row found last (`JOIN staff m ON m.id = c.manager_id`).

To ask about whole branches, such as everyone below each manager, make pairs: anchor every person as their own `top`, and keep the `top` while walking down. Then group by it.

challenges.title: Hard: Team sizes
challenges.promptMarkdown: For every staff member, show `name` and how many people are below them, directly or further down (`below`, 0 for those with nobody). Sort by below (most first), then name.
challenges.hint: Pairs: anchor `SELECT id AS top, id FROM staff`; walk down keeping `top`. Every pair except (top, top) is someone below. Count per top, from staff with a LEFT JOIN.
challenges.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE pairs(top, id) AS (
  SELECT id, id FROM staff
  UNION ALL
  SELECT p.top, s.id
  FROM staff s
  JOIN pairs p ON s.manager_id = p.id
)
SELECT st.name, COUNT(p.id) AS below
FROM staff st
LEFT JOIN pairs p ON p.top = st.id AND p.id <> st.id
GROUP BY st.id, st.name
ORDER BY below DESC, st.name;

challenges.hint: Use the pairs from Team sizes (including each person with themselves), join sales on `s.staff_id = p.id`, and group by top. Keep only those who have someone below.
challenges.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE pairs(top, id) AS (
  SELECT id, id FROM staff
  UNION ALL
  SELECT p.top, s.id
  FROM staff s
  JOIN pairs p ON s.manager_id = p.id
)
SELECT st.name, SUM(sa.quantity) AS team_items
FROM pairs p
JOIN staff st ON st.id = p.top
JOIN sales sa ON sa.staff_id = p.id
WHERE p.top IN (SELECT manager_id FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL)
GROUP BY st.id, st.name
ORDER BY team_items DESC, st.name;

challenges.title: Expert: Rolled-up takings
challenges.promptMarkdown: For every category, show `category` (its name) and the takings of all products in it or in any category inside it (`takings`, 2 decimals, 0 when none). Sort by category.
challenges.hint: Pairs again, on categories: (top, id). Join products on `pr.category_id = p.id`, LEFT JOIN sales, and sum quantity times price per top. COALESCE to 0.
challenges.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE pairs(top, id) AS (
  SELECT id, id FROM categories
  UNION ALL
  SELECT p.top, c.id
  FROM categories c
  JOIN pairs p ON c.parent_id = p.id
)
SELECT c.name AS category,
       ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(s.quantity * pr.price), 0), 2) AS takings
FROM categories c
JOIN pairs p ON p.top = c.id
LEFT JOIN products pr ON pr.category_id = p.id
LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.product_id = pr.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY category;

intro.title: Filling the gaps
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`GROUP BY sold_on` gives one row for each day that has sales. Days with no sales simply aren't there, so a report or a chart would skip them, and a moving average over "the last three rows" would really cover more than three days.

The fix is a **calendar**: make every day with a recursive CTE, then LEFT JOIN the data to it. Days with no sales keep their row, with NULLs from sales:

```
WITH RECURSIVE days(day) AS (
  SELECT MIN(sold_on) FROM sales
  UNION ALL
  SELECT date(day, '+1 day') FROM days
  WHERE day < (SELECT MAX(sold_on) FROM sales)
)
SELECT d.day, COUNT(s.id) AS sales
FROM days d
LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.sold_on = d.day
GROUP BY d.day
ORDER BY d.day;
```

`COUNT(s.id)` counts only matching sales, so an empty day gets 0. Sums are NULL on an empty day, so wrap them: `COALESCE(SUM(s.quantity), 0)`.

With every day present, the rest is easy: `WHERE s.id IS NULL` finds the empty days, `strftime('%w', d.day)` gives the weekday (0 is Sunday), and window functions over the calendar really do cover days, not just the days that happened to have rows.

The same trick works for any series with gaps: numbers, months or weeks. Make the full series first, then join.

GROUP BY d.day
ORDER BY d.day;

intro.title: Rows into columns
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A grouped query gives one row per group: items per product and week would be one row for each product and each week. Reports often want the weeks side by side instead, as columns. Turning rows into columns like that is called a **pivot**.

SQLite has no PIVOT keyword. You write one column for each value you want, each adding up only its own rows with `CASE`:

```
SELECT p.name,
       SUM(CASE WHEN s.sold_on < '2026-10-08' THEN s.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS week1,
       SUM(CASE WHEN s.sold_on >= '2026-10-08' THEN s.quantity ELSE 0 END) AS week2
FROM sales s
JOIN products p ON p.id = s.product_id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY p.name;
```

`ELSE 0` makes a product with no sales in a week show 0 rather than NULL. The other aggregates work too: `COUNT(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 END)` counts, because COUNT skips the NULL from a CASE with no ELSE.

A shorter way to write the condition is `FILTER`, after any aggregate:

```
SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE role = 'manager') AS managers,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE role = 'supervisor') AS supervisors,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE role = 'assistant') AS assistants,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE role = 'trainee') AS trainees
FROM staff;
```

With no GROUP BY, that is one row for the whole table. One limit of pivots in SQL: you must list the columns yourself, so you need to know the values (the weeks, the roles) when you write the query.

intro.title: Columns into rows
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`targets` is **wide**: one column per quarter. That is easy to read, but hard to query. To find each person's best quarter, or the total of all targets per quarter, you would have to write the same thing four times. A **long** table, one row per person and quarter, is much easier: then it's an ordinary GROUP BY.

The plain way to turn columns into rows is one SELECT per column, joined with `UNION ALL`:

```
SELECT staff_id, 'q1' AS quarter, q1 AS target FROM targets
UNION ALL SELECT staff_id, 'q2', q2 FROM targets
UNION ALL SELECT staff_id, 'q3', q3 FROM targets
UNION ALL SELECT staff_id, 'q4', q4 FROM targets
ORDER BY staff_id, quarter;
```

Another way is to join every row to a list of the quarters and pick the right column with CASE. `VALUES` makes the list without a table:

```
WITH quarters(quarter) AS (VALUES (1), (2), (3), (4))
SELECT t.staff_id, q.quarter,
       CASE q.quarter WHEN 1 THEN t.q1 WHEN 2 THEN t.q2 WHEN 3 THEN t.q3 ELSE t.q4 END AS target
FROM targets t
CROSS JOIN quarters q
WHERE target IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY t.staff_id, q.quarter;
```

`CROSS JOIN` pairs every target row with every quarter: 4 rows for each person. The CASE picks the column that goes with the quarter. Empty quarters come out as NULL targets, so filter them out, or keep them if the gaps matter.

Once the data is long, put it in a CTE and query it like any table: group it, rank it, or run windows over it.

challenges.title: Hard: Best quarter
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each staff member's highest quarter target: `name`, `quarter` (a number; the earlier one on a tie) and `target`. Sort by name.
challenges.hint: ROW_NUMBER per person over the long rows, `ORDER BY target DESC, quarter`; keep 1. NULLs sort last with DESC.
challenges.solution:
WITH quarters(quarter) AS (VALUES (1), (2), (3), (4))
, long AS (
  SELECT t.staff_id, q.quarter,
         CASE q.quarter WHEN 1 THEN t.q1 WHEN 2 THEN t.q2 WHEN 3 THEN t.q3 ELSE t.q4 END AS target
  FROM targets t
  CROSS JOIN quarters q
)
, ranked AS (
  SELECT staff_id, quarter, target,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY staff_id ORDER BY target DESC, quarter) AS n
  FROM long
  WHERE target IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT s.name, r.quarter, r.target
FROM ranked r
JOIN staff s ON s.id = r.staff_id
WHERE r.n = 1
ORDER BY s.name;

challenges.title: Hard: Quarter on quarter
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each quarter with a target, show `staff_id`, `quarter`, `target` and the rise since that person's previous quarter with a target (`rise`; empty for their first). Sort by staff_id, then quarter.
challenges.hint: Long rows without the NULLs, then `target - LAG(target) OVER (PARTITION BY staff_id ORDER BY quarter)`.
challenges.solution:
WITH quarters(quarter) AS (VALUES (1), (2), (3), (4))
, long AS (
  SELECT t.staff_id, q.quarter,
         CASE q.quarter WHEN 1 THEN t.q1 WHEN 2 THEN t.q2 WHEN 3 THEN t.q3 ELSE t.q4 END AS target
  FROM targets t
  CROSS JOIN quarters q
)
SELECT staff_id, quarter, target,
       target - LAG(target) OVER (PARTITION BY staff_id ORDER BY quarter) AS rise
FROM long
WHERE target IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY staff_id, quarter;

challenges.title: Expert: Halves
challenges.promptMarkdown: Go long and back again: for each `staff_id`, show the targets of the first half-year (`first_half`, Q1 and Q2) and second half (`second_half`), treating empty quarters as 0. Sort by staff_id.
challenges.hint: Long rows, then a pivot: `SUM(CASE WHEN quarter <= 2 THEN COALESCE(target, 0) ELSE 0 END)`.
challenges.solution:
WITH quarters(quarter) AS (VALUES (1), (2), (3), (4))
, long AS (
  SELECT t.staff_id, q.quarter,
         CASE q.quarter WHEN 1 THEN t.q1 WHEN 2 THEN t.q2 WHEN 3 THEN t.q3 ELSE t.q4 END AS target
  FROM targets t
  CROSS JOIN quarters q
)
SELECT staff_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN quarter <= 2 THEN COALESCE(target, 0) ELSE 0 END) AS first_half,
       SUM(CASE WHEN quarter > 2 THEN COALESCE(target, 0) ELSE 0 END) AS second_half
FROM long
GROUP BY staff_id
ORDER BY staff_id;

challenges.title: Expert: When targets start
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each staff member with targets, show `name`, their first quarter with a target (`first_quarter`) and how many quarters have one (`quarters`). Sort by first_quarter, then name.
challenges.hint: On the long rows without NULLs: `MIN(quarter)` and `COUNT(*)` per person.
challenges.solution:
WITH quarters(quarter) AS (VALUES (1), (2), (3), (4))
, long AS (
  SELECT t.staff_id, q.quarter,
         CASE q.quarter WHEN 1 THEN t.q1 WHEN 2 THEN t.q2 WHEN 3 THEN t.q3 ELSE t.q4 END AS target
  FROM targets t
  CROSS JOIN quarters q
)
SELECT s.name, MIN(l.quarter) AS first_quarter, COUNT(*) AS quarters
FROM long l
JOIN staff s ON s.id = l.staff_id
WHERE l.target IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY s.id, s.name
ORDER BY first_quarter, s.name;

intro.title: JSON in a column
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Products are not all alike: plants have a colour, a height and care needs, tools have a material. Instead of a column for every possible fact, `products.details` holds them as **JSON** text, such as `{"colour":"purple","height_cm":45,"tags":["scented","sun"],"care":{"water":"low","light":"sun"}}`.

`json_extract(details, '$.colour')` reads one value. The **path** starts at `$`, the whole value; `.colour` picks a key, `.care.water` goes inside an object, and `[0]` picks from an array: `$.tags[0]` is the first tag.

```
SELECT name,
       json_extract(details, '$.colour') AS colour,
       json_extract(details, '$.care.water') AS water,
       json_extract(details, '$.tags[0]') AS first_tag
FROM products
ORDER BY name;
```

A key that isn't there gives NULL, and so does NULL details, so tools simply have no colour. Numbers come back as numbers and text as text, so you can compare, sort and do sums with them. (Newer SQLite also has a short form, `details ->> '$.colour'`.)

JSON can be built too. `json_object('name', name, 'price', price)` makes an object from pairs of keys and values, and `json_array(1, 2)` makes an array.

To change one value inside the JSON, UPDATE the column with `json_set(details, '$.colour', 'red')`, which returns the JSON with that key set (added if it was missing). `json_remove(details, '$.tags')` returns it with a key taken out.

       ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS average_price
FROM products
WHERE json_extract(details, '$.colour') IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY colour
ORDER BY colour;

intro.title: JSON arrays and json_each
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Each product's `tags` is a JSON array. `json_array_length(details, '$.tags')` says how many tags there are. To work with the tags themselves, turn the array into rows with `json_each`:

```
SELECT p.name, t.value AS tag
FROM products p, json_each(p.details, '$.tags') AS t
ORDER BY p.name, tag;
```

`json_each` is a **table-valued function**: it goes in FROM like a table, and gives one row per element of the array, with the element in its `value` column (there are also `key`, the position, and `type`). Listing it after `products p,` joins each product to its own tags; a product with no tags, or no details, has no rows.

Once the tags are rows, everything else works on them: count products per tag, find products with a given tag, or join tags to sales:

```
SELECT t.value AS tag, COUNT(*) AS products
FROM products p, json_each(p.details, '$.tags') AS t
GROUP BY tag
ORDER BY products DESC, tag;
```

To test for one tag, use EXISTS: `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM json_each(details, '$.tags') WHERE value = 'easy')`.

The other way round, aggregates build JSON from rows. `json_group_array(name)` collects a group's values into one JSON array, and `json_group_object(name, price)` into one object. The values go in the order the rows arrive, so to control it, sort in a subquery first.

intro.title: Reading a query plan
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Before running a query, SQLite decides how: which table to read first, and whether to read every row or jump to the right ones with an index. Put `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` in front of a query to see that **plan** instead of the result:

```
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT * FROM sales WHERE product_id = 5;
```

The `detail` column is the part to read. `SCAN sales` means it reads every row of sales. With an index on `product_id`, the plan becomes `SEARCH sales USING INDEX sales_product (product_id=?)`: it looks the value up in the index and reads only the matching rows.

```
CREATE INDEX sales_product ON sales (product_id);

EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT * FROM sales WHERE product_id = 5;
```

Other things you will see: `SEARCH products USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)` is a lookup by id, the fastest kind. `USING COVERING INDEX` means the index holds every column the query needs, so the table isn't read at all. `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY` means SQLite sorts the rows itself; an index in the right order avoids that.

An index only helps when the query compares the column itself. `WHERE date(sold_on) = '2026-10-07'` can't use an index on sold_on (it would need the value of `date(sold_on)` for every row), but `WHERE sold_on = '2026-10-07'` can. The same goes for `LIKE '%…'` with a % at the start.

These tables are tiny, so every plan is fast here. On tables with millions of rows, SCAN against SEARCH is the difference between seconds and milliseconds. The plan is the first thing to look at when a query is slow.

intro.title: NULL and other traps
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Some queries look right, run without an error and still give the wrong answer. Most of these traps involve NULL. Here is the worst one: which staff have never made a sale?

```
SELECT name FROM staff
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT staff_id FROM sales)
ORDER BY name;
```

It returns nothing, though Rosa has made no sales. Self-checkout sales have a NULL `staff_id`, and `x NOT IN (…, NULL)` is never true: it asks "is x different from every value?", and nobody knows whether x differs from an unknown. Use `NOT EXISTS`, which isn't fooled by NULLs, or filter the NULLs out of the subquery.

The other NULL traps: `= NULL` is never true, so use `IS NULL`. `COUNT(column)`, `SUM` and `AVG` skip NULLs, while `COUNT(*)` counts rows. Anything combined with NULL is NULL: `price * 2`, and `'Hi ' || NULL` too. A sum of no rows is NULL, not 0. And in SQLite, NULLs sort first in ascending order.

A LEFT JOIN can be undone by WHERE. In `products p LEFT JOIN sales s ON … WHERE s.sold_on >= '2026-10-08'`, products with no sales then have NULL there and the WHERE removes them. A condition on the right-hand table belongs in the ON clause.

One more that isn't about NULL: dividing a whole number by a whole number gives a whole number in SQLite. `7 / 2` is 3. Write `7 * 1.0 / 2`, or `7 / 2.0`, to get 3.5.

challenges.title: Easy: Never sold
challenges.promptMarkdown: This should list the staff who have never made a sale, but it returns nothing. Fix it. Sort by name.
challenges.hint: Use `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sales s WHERE s.staff_id = st.id)`, or add `WHERE staff_id IS NOT NULL` inside the subquery.

challenges.promptMarkdown: Show one row: the number of sales (`all_sales`), the sales served by staff (`staffed`) and the self-checkout sales (`self_checkout`).

challenges.solution:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_sales, COUNT(staff_id) AS staffed, COUNT(*) - COUNT(staff_id) AS self_checkout
FROM sales;

challenges.title: Medium: Keep every product
challenges.promptMarkdown: This should show every product with the items sold from 2026-10-08 on (`items`, 0 if none), but products with no such sales vanish. Fix it. Sort by name.
challenges.starterCode:
SELECT p.name, COALESCE(SUM(s.quantity), 0) AS items
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.product_id = p.id
WHERE s.sold_on >= '2026-10-08'
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY p.name;
challenges.hint: Move the date condition into the ON clause: `ON s.product_id = p.id AND s.sold_on >= '2026-10-08'`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT p.name, COALESCE(SUM(s.quantity), 0) AS items
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.product_id = p.id AND s.sold_on >= '2026-10-08'
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY p.name;

challenges.title: Medium: Items per sale
challenges.promptMarkdown: This should show each sold product's average items per sale (`per_sale`, 2 decimals), but every answer is a whole number. Fix it. Sort by name.
challenges.starterCode:
SELECT p.name, ROUND(SUM(s.quantity) / COUNT(*), 2) AS per_sale
FROM sales s
JOIN products p ON p.id = s.product_id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY p.name;
challenges.hint: Whole number divided by whole number is a whole number. Multiply by 1.0 first.
challenges.solution:
SELECT p.name, ROUND(SUM(s.quantity) * 1.0 / COUNT(*), 2) AS per_sale
FROM sales s
JOIN products p ON p.id = s.product_id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY p.name;

challenges.promptMarkdown: This should label everyone as `Name (manager's name)`, but the person at the top gets an empty label. Fix it so they get `Name (no manager)`. Sort by name.

SELECT s.name, s.name || ' (' || m.name || ')' AS label
FROM staff s

ORDER BY s.name;
challenges.hint: Text joined with NULL is NULL. `COALESCE(m.name, 'no manager')`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT s.name, s.name || ' (' || COALESCE(m.name, 'no manager') || ')' AS label
FROM staff s
LEFT JOIN staff m ON m.id = s.manager_id
ORDER BY s.name;

challenges.title: Hard: Two averages
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show one row with the average Q1 target of those who have one (`avg_set`) and the average if empty Q1 targets count as 0 (`avg_all`), both 1 decimal.
challenges.hint: `AVG(q1)` skips NULLs; `AVG(COALESCE(q1, 0))` doesn't.
challenges.solution:

challenges.title: Hard: Missing prices last
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show every product's `name` and `price`, cheapest first, but with products without a price at the end. Then by name.
challenges.hint: NULLs sort first. `ORDER BY price IS NULL, price, name` puts them last (0 sorts before 1). Newer SQLite also has `NULLS LAST`.

challenges.title: Expert: Takings for everyone
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show every staff member's `name` and `takings` (quantity times price of their sales, 2 decimals), with 0 for anyone with none. Most first, then by name.
challenges.hint: LEFT JOIN sales and products; `ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(s.quantity * p.price), 0), 2)`. A sale of a product with no price adds nothing.
challenges.solution:
SELECT st.name, ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(s.quantity * p.price), 0), 2) AS takings
FROM staff st
LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.staff_id = st.id
LEFT JOIN products p ON p.id = s.product_id
GROUP BY st.id, st.name
ORDER BY takings DESC, st.name;

challenges.title: Expert: Tills open
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each `sold_on`, show how many different staff sold something (`staff`) and how many tills were used (`tills`), counting the self-checkout as one till and each staff member as one. In date order.
challenges.hint: `COUNT(DISTINCT staff_id)` skips the NULLs. For tills, turn NULL into a value that is no staff id: `COUNT(DISTINCT COALESCE(staff_id, 0))`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT sold_on, COUNT(DISTINCT staff_id) AS staff, COUNT(DISTINCT COALESCE(staff_id, 0)) AS tills
FROM sales
GROUP BY sold_on
ORDER BY sold_on;

intro.title: Easy project: Staff directory
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The garden centre wants a staff directory for its notice board and intranet: who everyone reports to, how long they have been here, how the teams are arranged, and an org chart that stays up to date by itself.

Today is 2026-10-24.
intro.sandboxCode:
SELECT s.name, s.role, m.name AS manager
FROM staff s
LEFT JOIN staff m ON m.id = s.manager_id
ORDER BY s.name;

challenges.title: Easy: Directory view
challenges.promptMarkdown: Create a view `directory` with each staff member's `name`, `role` and their manager's name (`manager`; `none` for the person at the top).
challenges.hint: A self LEFT JOIN with `COALESCE(m.name, 'none') AS manager`.
challenges.solution:
CREATE VIEW directory AS
SELECT s.name, s.role, COALESCE(m.name, 'none') AS manager
FROM staff s
LEFT JOIN staff m ON m.id = s.manager_id;

tests.label: The directory view has the right columns
tests.assertion: SELECT name FROM pragma_table_info('directory') ORDER BY cid

tests.label: The directory view gives the right rows
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM directory ORDER BY name

challenges.title: Easy: Years of service
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each staff member's `name`, `hired` date and whole years of service up to today (`years`). Longest first, then by name.
challenges.hint: `CAST((julianday('2026-10-24') - julianday(hired)) / 365.25 AS INTEGER) AS years`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT name, hired,
       CAST((julianday('2026-10-24') - julianday(hired)) / 365.25 AS INTEGER) AS years
FROM staff
ORDER BY years DESC, name;

challenges.title: Medium: Levels
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each staff member's `name`, `role` and `level` in the tree (1 at the top). Sort by level, then name.
challenges.hint: A recursive CTE from the person with no manager, joining `s.manager_id = c.id`.
challenges.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE chart(id, level) AS (
  SELECT id, 1 FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.id, c.level + 1
  FROM staff s
  JOIN chart c ON s.manager_id = c.id
)
SELECT s.name, s.role, c.level
FROM chart c
JOIN staff s ON s.id = c.id
ORDER BY c.level, s.name;

challenges.title: Medium: Direct reports
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each staff member who manages someone, show `name` and how many people report straight to them (`direct_reports`). Most first, then by name.
challenges.hint: Join staff to itself on `r.manager_id = m.id` and count per manager.
challenges.solution:
SELECT m.name, COUNT(*) AS direct_reports
FROM staff m
JOIN staff r ON r.manager_id = m.id
GROUP BY m.id, m.name
ORDER BY direct_reports DESC, m.name;

challenges.title: Hard: Whole teams
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each staff member who manages someone, show `name` and how many people are in their whole team below them (`team_size`). Most first, then by name.
challenges.hint: Make (top, id) pairs by anchoring every person and walking down; count the pairs where id isn't top.
challenges.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE pairs(top, id) AS (
  SELECT id, id FROM staff
  UNION ALL
  SELECT p.top, s.id
  FROM staff s
  JOIN pairs p ON s.manager_id = p.id
)
SELECT st.name, COUNT(*) AS team_size
FROM pairs p
JOIN staff st ON st.id = p.top
WHERE p.id <> p.top
GROUP BY st.id, st.name
ORDER BY team_size DESC, st.name;

challenges.title: Hard: Org chart view
challenges.promptMarkdown: Create a view `org_chart` with each staff member's `name`, `level` (1 at the top) and `path` (names from the top down joined with `/`). A view can hold a recursive WITH.
challenges.hint: `CREATE VIEW org_chart AS WITH RECURSIVE chart(…) AS (…) SELECT name, level, path FROM chart;`
challenges.solution:
CREATE VIEW org_chart AS
WITH RECURSIVE chart(id, name, level, path) AS (
  SELECT id, name, 1, name FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.id, s.name, c.level + 1, c.path || '/' || s.name
  FROM staff s
  JOIN chart c ON s.manager_id = c.id
)
SELECT name, level, path FROM chart;

tests.label: The org_chart view gives the right rows

intro.title: Medium project: Product catalogue
intro.bodyMarkdown: The website needs a catalogue built from the products table: names with their categories and colours, a tag index, a care table, a price list as JSON for the web page, category paths, and a restock flag in the details.

challenges.title: Easy: Catalogue
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show every product's `name`, its category name (`category`; `none` if it has none), `price` and `colour` from the details. Sort by name.
challenges.hint: LEFT JOIN categories, `COALESCE(c.name, 'none')`, and `json_extract(p.details, '$.colour')`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT p.name, COALESCE(c.name, 'none') AS category, p.price,
       json_extract(p.details, '$.colour') AS colour
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN categories c ON c.id = p.category_id
ORDER BY p.name;

challenges.title: Medium: Tag index
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each tag, show `tag`, the number of products with it (`products`) and the cheapest price among them (`from_price`). Sort by tag.
challenges.hint: `FROM products p, json_each(p.details, '$.tags') AS t`, grouped by `t.value`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT t.value AS tag, COUNT(*) AS products, MIN(p.price) AS from_price
FROM products p, json_each(p.details, '$.tags') AS t
GROUP BY tag
ORDER BY tag;

challenges.title: Medium: Care table
challenges.promptMarkdown: For each light need (`light`), show how many products need `low`, `medium` and `high` water, as columns `low`, `medium` and `high`. Only products with care details. Sort by light.
challenges.hint: Group by the extracted light, and `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE json_extract(details, '$.care.water') = 'low')` for each column.
challenges.solution:
SELECT json_extract(details, '$.care.light') AS light,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE json_extract(details, '$.care.water') = 'low') AS low,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE json_extract(details, '$.care.water') = 'medium') AS medium,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE json_extract(details, '$.care.water') = 'high') AS high
FROM products
WHERE json_extract(details, '$.care') IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY light
ORDER BY light;

challenges.title: Medium: Price list as JSON
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show one value, `price_list`: a JSON array with an object for each priced product, like `{"name":"Lavender","price":6.5}`, cheapest first, then by name.
challenges.hint: `json_group_array(json_object('name', name, 'price', price))` over a sorted subquery.
challenges.solution:
SELECT json_group_array(json_object('name', name, 'price', price)) AS price_list
FROM (SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price IS NOT NULL ORDER BY price, name);

challenges.title: Hard: Category paths
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show each category's full `path` (like `Plants > Outdoor plants > Shrubs`) and how many products are in that category itself (`products`, 0 if none). Sort by path.
challenges.hint: Build the paths with a recursive CTE, then LEFT JOIN products on the category id and count.
challenges.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE tree(id, path) AS (
  SELECT id, name FROM categories WHERE parent_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, t.path || ' > ' || c.name
  FROM categories c
  JOIN tree t ON c.parent_id = t.id
)
SELECT t.path, COUNT(p.id) AS products
FROM tree t
LEFT JOIN products p ON p.category_id = t.id
GROUP BY t.id, t.path
ORDER BY t.path;

challenges.title: Hard: Restock flags
challenges.promptMarkdown: Add `"restock": true` to the details of every product that sold 4 or more items in all. (Products with no details yet get `{"restock":true}`.)
challenges.hint: `json_set(COALESCE(details, '{}'), '$.restock', json('true'))`, `WHERE id IN (SELECT product_id FROM sales GROUP BY product_id HAVING SUM(quantity) >= 4)`.

challenges.title: Medium: Every day
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show every `day` with its number of `sales` and `items` (0 on days with none). In date order.
challenges.hint: A calendar CTE, LEFT JOIN sales, `COUNT(s.id)` and `COALESCE(SUM(s.quantity), 0)`.
challenges.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE days(day) AS (
  SELECT MIN(sold_on) FROM sales
  UNION ALL
  SELECT date(day, '+1 day') FROM days
  WHERE day < (SELECT MAX(sold_on) FROM sales)
)
SELECT d.day, COUNT(s.id) AS sales, COALESCE(SUM(s.quantity), 0) AS items
FROM days d
LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.sold_on = d.day
GROUP BY d.day
ORDER BY d.day;

challenges.title: Hard: Daily report view
challenges.promptMarkdown: Create a view `daily_report` with every `day`, its `takings` (2 decimals, 0 if none) and the running takings so far (`takings_so_far`, 2 decimals).
challenges.hint: Put the calendar CTE inside the view; LEFT JOIN sales and products; a running SUM over the grouped days.
challenges.solution:
CREATE VIEW daily_report AS
WITH RECURSIVE days(day) AS (
  SELECT MIN(sold_on) FROM sales
  UNION ALL
  SELECT date(day, '+1 day') FROM days
  WHERE day < (SELECT MAX(sold_on) FROM sales)
)
SELECT d.day,
       ROUND(COALESCE(SUM(s.quantity * p.price), 0), 2) AS takings,
       ROUND(SUM(COALESCE(SUM(s.quantity * p.price), 0)) OVER (ORDER BY d.day), 2) AS takings_so_far
FROM days d
LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.sold_on = d.day
LEFT JOIN products p ON p.id = s.product_id
GROUP BY d.day;

challenges.title: Hard: Weekend table
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show every staff member's `name`, the items they sold on weekdays (`weekday_items`) and at weekends (`weekend_items`), 0 where none. Most items in all first, then by name.
challenges.hint: LEFT JOIN sales to staff; `COALESCE(SUM(s.quantity) FILTER (WHERE strftime('%w', s.sold_on) IN ('0', '6')), 0)`; sort by `weekday_items + weekend_items DESC`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT st.name,
       COALESCE(SUM(s.quantity) FILTER (WHERE strftime('%w', s.sold_on) NOT IN ('0', '6')), 0) AS weekday_items,
       COALESCE(SUM(s.quantity) FILTER (WHERE strftime('%w', s.sold_on) IN ('0', '6')), 0) AS weekend_items
FROM staff st
LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.staff_id = st.id
GROUP BY st.id, st.name
ORDER BY weekday_items + weekend_items DESC, st.name;

challenges.title: Hard: Self-checkout share
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show every `day`, its `items`, the self-checkout items (`self_items`) and their share (`self_pct`, %, 1 decimal; empty on days with no items). In date order.
challenges.hint: `SUM(s.quantity) FILTER (WHERE s.staff_id IS NULL)` for the self-checkout; divide by `NULLIF(items, 0)` so empty days give NULL instead of an error-free 0.
challenges.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE days(day) AS (
  SELECT MIN(sold_on) FROM sales
  UNION ALL
  SELECT date(day, '+1 day') FROM days
  WHERE day < (SELECT MAX(sold_on) FROM sales)
)
, daily AS (
  SELECT d.day,
         COALESCE(SUM(s.quantity), 0) AS items,
         COALESCE(SUM(s.quantity) FILTER (WHERE s.id IS NOT NULL AND s.staff_id IS NULL), 0) AS self_items
  FROM days d
  LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.sold_on = d.day
  GROUP BY d.day
)
SELECT day, items, self_items, ROUND(100.0 * self_items / NULLIF(items, 0), 1) AS self_pct
FROM daily
ORDER BY day;

challenges.title: Hard: Keep the report fast
challenges.promptMarkdown: The report groups sales by day and adds up quantities. Create an index called `sales_day_quantity` on `sales (sold_on, quantity)` so that `SELECT sold_on, SUM(quantity) FROM sales GROUP BY sold_on` is answered from the index alone.
challenges.hint: A covering index holds every column the query reads, so list both columns in the index, in the order given.
challenges.solution: CREATE INDEX sales_day_quantity ON sales (sold_on, quantity);

challenges.title: Hard: Best day of each week
challenges.promptMarkdown: Split the days into weeks of 7 from the first sale (`week` 1, 2, …). For each week, show its best day or days by items: `week`, `day` and `items`. Sort by week, then day.
challenges.hint: `CAST((julianday(d.day) - julianday((SELECT MIN(sold_on) FROM sales))) / 7 AS INTEGER) + 1 AS week`. Then RANK within each week by items, and keep 1.
challenges.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE days(day) AS (
  SELECT MIN(sold_on) FROM sales
  UNION ALL
  SELECT date(day, '+1 day') FROM days
  WHERE day < (SELECT MAX(sold_on) FROM sales)
)
, daily AS (
  SELECT d.day,
         CAST((julianday(d.day) - julianday((SELECT MIN(sold_on) FROM sales))) / 7 AS INTEGER) + 1 AS week,
         COALESCE(SUM(s.quantity), 0) AS items
  FROM days d
  LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.sold_on = d.day
  GROUP BY d.day
),
ranked AS (
  SELECT week, day, items, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY week ORDER BY items DESC) AS place
  FROM daily
)
SELECT week, day, items
FROM ranked
WHERE place = 1
ORDER BY week, day;
